title: Notification System
seoTitle: Design a Notification System (Push, Email, SMS)
description: Design a multi-channel notification system — push, email and SMS — with user preferences, reliable delivery, retries, deduplication and rate limiting.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Notification System?
blocks.text: A notification system is a shared platform that lets internal services send messages to users over push, email and SMS without each team integrating with providers themselves.

items: Internal services should be able to send a notification to a user (or many users) via push, email or SMS.
Users should be able to set preferences — opt out of channels or categories (e.g. marketing).
Services should be able to schedule notifications for a future time.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Notifications must be delivered at least once — none should be silently lost.
Transactional notifications (OTP codes, payments) should arrive within seconds; marketing can be slower.
The system should handle 10M notifications per minute during campaign bursts.
Users shouldn't receive duplicates or be spammed.

blocks.text: The system is a pipeline: accept a request, resolve who and how to reach, then deliver through third-party providers (APNs, FCM, SES/SendGrid, Twilio). We'll make each step durable and independently scalable.

items: **Notification**: the request — recipient(s), template, data, priority, category, schedule.
**Preference**: a user's opt-ins per channel and category.
**Device / Contact**: push tokens, email address, phone number.
**Delivery**: one attempt to send one notification over one channel, with status.

blocks.text: 1) Services should be able to send a notification
The **Notification Service** validates the request, stores it, and immediately returns `202 Accepted`. Work then flows through queues so a slow provider never blocks callers.
2) Users should be able to set preferences

The **Router** reads the user's preferences (cached in Redis, since every notification needs them) and drops channels or categories the user has opted out of. It then renders the template per channel and looks up contact details and device tokens.
3) Services should be able to schedule notifications
Scheduled notifications are stored with a `sendAt` time and released into the queue when due, using a delayed-delivery mechanism like the one in the Job Scheduler problem.
1) How do we guarantee at-least-once delivery?

blocks.title: Call providers synchronously from the API

approach.text: The Notification Service calls APNs, SES and Twilio directly before responding.

challenges.text: Provider latency and outages leak into every caller; if the process crashes mid-send, the notification is lost.

blocks.title: Durable queues per channel with retries and a DLQ

approach.text: Persist the notification first, then enqueue. Each channel (push, email, SMS) has its own queue and worker pool so an SMS provider outage doesn't back up push. Workers acknowledge only after the provider accepts the message; failures retry with exponential backoff and eventually land in a dead-letter queue for inspection.

challenges.text: Retries mean the same message can be sent twice — handled by deduplication below.

blocks.text: 2) How do we avoid duplicate notifications?

Callers include an **idempotency key**; the Notification Service stores it with a unique constraint and returns the existing notification on a repeat request. Channel workers record a `Delivery` row keyed by `(notificationId, userId, channel)` and skip sending if it's already `SENT`. This makes both API retries and worker retries safe.
3) How do we handle campaign bursts without delaying critical messages?

challenges.text: A 50M-recipient marketing blast sits in front of an OTP code, which then arrives minutes late.

approach.text: Separate **high-priority** (transactional) and **bulk** queues per channel, with dedicated capacity for high priority. Expand campaigns asynchronously in batches. Respect provider rate limits with a token bucket per provider, and enforce per-user frequency caps (e.g. at most 3 marketing pushes a day).

challenges.text: Requires classifying every notification correctly — the API's `category` field drives routing.

blocks.text: Clean up dead push tokens: APNs and FCM tell you when a token is invalid. Deleting them avoids wasting sends and keeps provider reputation healthy.

quiz.question: Why should the API return 202 Accepted and send asynchronously?
options: Provider latency and outages shouldn't block callers or lose messages
quiz.explanation: Persisting and queueing decouples callers from slow, failure-prone third-party providers.

quiz.question: What prevents a retried API request from sending the same notification twice?
options: An idempotency key with a unique constraint
quiz.explanation: The repeat request maps to the existing notification instead of creating a new one.

quiz.question: How do you stop a marketing blast from delaying OTP codes?
options: Separate high-priority and bulk queues with dedicated capacity
quiz.explanation: Priority lanes keep transactional traffic flowing regardless of bulk backlog.

quiz.question: Why give each channel its own queue and worker pool?
options: To isolate failures, so an SMS outage doesn't back up push
quiz.explanation: Isolation keeps healthy channels flowing while a broken provider retries.
